opus-5.5.text:
I think about it on a few different time horizons, because the answer really changes depending on how far out you look.

In the near term, the next few years, I think we'll see humanoids move out of demo videos and into fairly structured settings: factories, warehouses, logistics. Not because those tasks are glamorous, but because the environment is somewhat predictable, the economic case is clear, and you can tolerate a robot that's a bit slower than a human as long as it works reliably for long shifts. The honest bottleneck right now isn't really the hardware anymore. Actuators, batteries, hands have all improved a lot. The bottleneck is generalization: getting a robot to handle the thousandth slightly different situation without someone re-engineering it.

That's where the medium-term story gets interesting. What happened with language models showed us that scale plus the right data can produce surprisingly general capabilities. The open question for robotics is whether we can build the equivalent data flywheel for physical interaction. We don't have an internet's worth of robot data lying around, so people are attacking it from many directions: simulation, teleoperation at scale, learning from human video, and so on. I suspect the answer will be a combination, and whoever figures out how to collect and use physical data most efficiently will have a real advantage.

And then the long term. I do believe the humanoid form factor makes sense, not because humans are the optimal design, but because our entire world is built around human bodies: stairs, door handles, tools, kitchens. A general-purpose robot that fits into that world without us rebuilding everything has enormous leverage. Over a couple of decades, I could see humanoids becoming something like a general-purpose labor platform, in homes, in elder care, in dangerous jobs.

But I'd add two cautions. First, timelines in robotics have historically been overly optimistic. The physical world is unforgiving in ways software isn't; a mistake isn't a wrong word, it's a dropped object or an injured person. So safety and reliability will set the pace more than raw capability. Second, the societal questions—labor displacement, who owns these systems, how they're deployed in private spaces like homes—are going to matter as much as the technical ones. I'd like to see the field think about those early rather than after the fact.

So overall I'm optimistic, but in a patient way. I think it's one of the most important technical problems of our generation, and it's going to take longer than the hype suggests, but probably arrive sooner than the skeptics expect.

r001.rationale: The response discusses near-, medium-, and long-term development, but does not describe the past fifty years as recurring waves.

r002.rationale: It does not compare the current wave with previous waves or predict that it will be larger.

r003.rationale: It notes current limits in generalization, safety, and reliability, but does not clearly judge the technology insufficient for every envisioned household scenario.

r004.rationale: It discusses several approaches to robotics data and a long development timeline, but does not say realizing the potential will require successive waves of product exploration.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. When I think about where humanoid robotics is heading long term, I try to separate the hype cycle from the actual trajectory, because right now those two things look very different.

The near term is honestly a bit disappointing if you only watch the demo videos. Most of what you see is teleoperation, or a policy that works in one lab setup and falls apart the moment the lighting changes. The hardware has gotten remarkably good over the past few years. Actuators, batteries, hands, the whole body stack has improved faster than I expected. But the bottleneck has shifted almost entirely to the intelligence layer, and that's the part people underestimate.

The real question for the next decade is data. Language models got to where they are because the internet was a free dataset of human text. There is no equivalent for physical manipulation. You can't scrape the internet for "how does it feel to grasp a wet dish." So the field is going through this scramble: teleop data collection farms, simulation with sim-to-real transfer, video pretraining from human demonstrations. My bet is that the winners won't be the ones with the best robot body. They'll be the ones who figure out the data flywheel, where deployed robots generate the data that improves the next model, and that loop compounds.

As for the humanoid form factor itself, I'm cautiously in favor, but not for the romantic reason. The argument is practical: the world was built for humans, so a human-shaped machine inherits all of that infrastructure for free. Stairs, door handles, tools, vehicles. The counterargument is that the humanoid is often the hardest and most expensive solution to a problem a wheeled base with an arm could solve. I think both will coexist for a long time. Factories and warehouses will adopt whatever is cheapest and most reliable, and early on that is usually not a humanoid. Homes are where the humanoid form really earns its place, because a home is an unstructured mess that no one is going to redesign for a robot.

If I zoom out to twenty or thirty years, I think the trajectory looks a lot like computing did. First expensive, specialized, in industrial settings. Then a long plateau where it's useful but not transformative. Then a sudden inflection when cost and capability cross some threshold and it becomes a general-purpose platform. I think we're in the first phase now and people are mistaking it for the third.

The thing I'd caution against is timelines. Every demo makes it look like we're two years away. We've been two years away for about fifteen years. The honest answer is that the foundational work on learning from physical interaction is still immature, and that's exactly why it's the most interesting place to be working right now.

r001.rationale: It describes recent hardware progress and a computing-like trajectory, but not recurring waves of humanoid robotics development over the past fifty years.

r002.rationale: It does not predict that the current wave will be larger than earlier waves.

r003.rationale: It calls homes unstructured and physical-learning work immature, but does not clearly judge current technology insufficient for every envisioned household scenario.

r004.rationale: It describes phases and a possible inflection point, but does not suggest that realizing humanoid robots’ potential will require successive waves of product exploration.

astra-6.text:
I think humanoid robotics has enormous long-term potential, but progress will come in stages. The first question is where these robots can do useful work reliably and at a reasonable cost. A compelling demonstration is one thing; operating every day in a real environment is much harder.

I expect early adoption in relatively structured settings, like factories and warehouses. Those deployments can help improve the hardware, train the systems, and reveal what actually breaks. Homes are a bigger challenge because they’re unpredictable, and robots need to work safely around people.

The appeal of the humanoid form is that our world is built for humans. But having a human-shaped body doesn’t automatically make a robot capable. Manipulation, learning, reliability, and cost all have to improve together.

So I’m optimistic about the direction, but cautious about precise timelines. The important milestone is when a robot becomes a useful tool that people can depend on.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the long-term potential is enormous, but the path will be gradual. A humanoid robot needs to do more than demonstrate an impressive movement. It needs to perform useful work reliably, safely, and at a cost that makes sense.

I expect the first meaningful deployments to involve relatively structured tasks, where you can define success clearly and recover when something goes wrong. As the hardware and intelligence improve, robots can take on a wider range of environments and responsibilities. Homes are an exciting possibility, but they’re also very challenging because almost everything is unpredictable.

The humanoid form is attractive because our world is designed around people. But having two arms and two legs isn’t the goal by itself. The goal is to build machines that can help people. Over the long term, I think progress will depend on how well we connect physical capability with the ability to learn, adapt, and understand the limits of what a robot can safely do.
